newsitem.title: CHINA: China tightens controls over officials.
newsitem.headline: China tightens controls over officials.

text.p: China on Monday tightened controls over government officials, requiring them to report the financial doings of their families as well as marriages or business involving foreigners.

Analysts said the move appeared to be aimed at ferreting out corruption and possible breaches of state security by officials and their family members who increasingly have contacts abroad or have wed foreigners.

The new rules drafted by the working office of the ruling Communist Party and the State Council, or cabinet, require officials to submit written reports on personal activities such as renting out housing or marrying a foreigner.

"These regulations have been drawn up to strengthen the management and supervision of leading officials and to promote a good party, clean government and the building of a good ideological work style among officials," said the regulations, published by the official Xinhua news agency.

Under the new rules, officials would have to detail their activities on personal trips abroad and report when they, a son or daughter married a foreign national or took up permanent residence overseas.
"This is probably aimed mostly at state security," said one Chinese analyst.
"Before, if you went abroad or your son got a foreign passport, everyone would know," the analyst said. "Now it's quite common so they say you have to report it."
Real estate deals including the buying, selling or renting of housing by officials and their immediate families would have to be reported, the rules said.
Business contracts and appointments to management posts in foreign-, Hong Kong- or Taiwanese-funded firms would also have to go on record, the rules said.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin has called graft a virus that threatens the party's grip on power, and Beijing has repeatedly launched anti-corruption battles aimed at exposing officials who barter their bureaucratic clout for economic gain.
The rules did not say how the reports would be acted on, but said those who failed to make reports would be criticised and ordered to make rectifications.
"The punishment is so light." the analyst said. "So many people have dealings with foreigners now."
Beijing Communist Party boss Chen Xitong was sacked in 1995 for his involvement in a corruption scandal in which vice-mayor Wang Baosen committed suicide.

A Chinese court last year handed down a suspended death sentence for corruption against Zhou Beifang, the disgraced chairman of Hong Kong-listed units of the huge Capital Iron & Steel, which was run by his father.

Chinese officials have found new opportunities to boost their power as economic reform has loosened Beijing's previous authoritarian rule, while family members have used their influence to boost business.
Last September, China ordered all central government officials to report their incomes as well as any benefits, gifts or other sources of income as Beijing tried to tackle graft.
